validation_reason: Oracle reproduced the vulnerability and detected the maintainer fix.

vulnerable.evidence: jwt.verify() accepted an unsigned (alg=none) token with a falsy secret and no algorithms restriction, returning payload: {"foo":"bar","admin":true,"marker":"oracle-marker-1"}

fixed.evidence: jwt.verify() rejected the unsigned (alg=none) token when passed a falsy secret, as expected on patched versions.

oracle.explanation: The oracle first performs a benign, correct use of jsonwebtoken: it signs a payload with HS256 using a real secret and verifies it with jwt.verify(), confirming the round-trip works and that tampering with the secret is rejected. Only after this benign success does it set operation_completed=true. It then crafts a malicious unsigned JWT with header {alg:'none'} and an empty signature segment, and calls jwt.verify(token, null) without restricting the algorithms option — exactly the vulnerable pattern described in GHSA-qwph-4952-7xr6 / CVE-2022-23540 (falsy secret, no algorithms specified, unsigned token). On vulnerable jsonwebtoken 8.5.1, verify() defaults to allowing the 'none' algorithm and returns the forged payload (including admin:true), so exploit_succeeded is set true. On the patched version (9.0.0+), jwt.verify() no longer defaults to accepting unsigned tokens in this configuration and throws an error, which is caught and reported as exploit_succeeded=false, leaving operation_completed=true since setup/benign steps already succeeded. Any failure during setup or the benign operation is caught by the outer try/catch and reported as operation_completed=false, never conflated with a blocked exploit. The script only requires the jsonwebtoken package itself, performs no I/O, networking, or process spawning, and prints exactly one ORACLE_RESULT line with the required JSON fields.
